news.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
news.description: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

medtech.title: The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
medtech.description: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging.

medtech.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
medtech.description: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection.

research.title: Longitudinal changes in cognitive biases mediate the association between stress exposure and psychotic-like experiences: Findings from a general population study.
research.abstract: Background Exposure to stress is a well-established risk factor for psychotic experiences, yet the cognitive mechanisms underlying this association remain insufficiently understood. This study examined whether longitudinal changes in cognitive biases mediate the relationship between stress exposure and changes in psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) in the general population sample of adults aged 18-40 years. Methods Adults without a history of psychiatric treatment were assessed at baseline and at 12-month follow-up. Change-score mediation models with bootstrap confidence intervals were estimated, adjusting for age, gender, and education. Results Of 5,126 adults who completed the baseline assessment, 2,290 (44.7%) participated in the follow-up. Greater stress exposure predicted increases in PLEs, negative, and depressive symptoms. After correction for multiple testing, significant indirect effects consistent with mediation by cognitive biases were observed for PLEs, but not for negative or depressive symptoms. These effects were significant for changes in belief inflexibility, safety behaviors, external attribution, and subjective cognitive and social cognitive problems, but not for attention to threat or jumping to conclusions. Reverse mediation models indicated consistently smaller indirect effects. In parallel multiple-mediator models, no individual bias showed a unique indirect effect on PLEs, yet the total indirect effect remained significant, suggesting mediation through interrelated biases. Social cognitive problems emerged as the only bias with a specific indirect effect on negative and depressive symptoms. Conclusions Longitudinal changes in cognitive biases might represent an indirect pathway to the association between stress exposure and increases in PLEs. These findings highlight cognitive biases as potential targets for preventive interventions.

research.title: Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging.
research.abstract: Severe mental disorders such as bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are characterized by reduced life expectancy, premature mortality and alterations of aging biomarkers, leading to hypothesize that they might be associated with accelerated cellular aging. We quantified the genetic overlap between severe mental disorders and a comprehensive set of aging biomarkers including multivariate longevity and healthy aging (mvAge), brain age gap (BAG), leucocyte telomere length (gLTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number and epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA) using cutting-edge methods, and evaluated their functional enrichment and suitability as drug targets. All disorders were negatively correlated with mvAge. Further, MDD correlated negatively with gLTL and positively with gEAA. We identified several pleiotropic variants, with nine genes (AC068490.2, ASIC2, CNNM2, FURIN, GPM6A, HS6ST3, RP5-1043L13.1, SORCS3 and SP4) containing variants shared between aging biomarkers and all disorders. Functional analyses with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization showed that increased expression of the druggable gene CRHR1 in the prefrontal cortex was associated with increased risk of MDD and BAG measures. Our findings suggest that shared heritability might contribute to reduced longevity and healthy aging in severe mental disorders and identify pleiotropic genes involved in synaptic function and metabolic processes related to micronutrients such as folate and magnesium.

research.title: Altered GABA B receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial.
research.abstract: Metabotropic γ-aminobutyric acid type B receptors (GABA B Rs) are implicated in alcohol use disorder (AUD) and represent a promising therapeutic target. However, robust biomarkers of GABA B Rs target engagement and sensitivity in humans are lacking. We examined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-derived cortical inhibition and growth hormone (GH) release as measures of GABA B R function, and whether heavy alcohol use is associated with altered responses to pharmacological GABA B R activation. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers) received baclofen 30 mg, baclofen 60 mg, or placebo across three sessions. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI), short-interval intracortical inhibition, and intracortical facilitation were assessed with paired-pulse TMS at baseline and ~60 min post-dose. Baclofen blood concentrations and plasma GH levels were measured. Baclofen produced dose-dependent increases in GH release, confirming neuroendocrine GABA B R engagement. The LICI response to baclofen differed between groups: In light drinkers, baclofen at 30 mg potentiated LICI, and a similar potentiation was seen at 60 mg, indicating that a plateau may have been reached. In contrast, in heavy drinkers, a potentiation of LICI similar to that in light drinkers was seen at 30 mg baclofen, but was absent at the 60 mg dose despite comparable pharmacokinetics, suggesting altered GABA B R function. Effects were selective for GABA B R-mediated inhibition, with no consistent modulation of short-interval intracortical inhibition or corticospinal excitability. Acute baclofen administration reveals altered GABA B R sensitivity in heavy drinkers, with preserved responses at lower doses but reduced response under stronger agonist stimulation. LICI and GH release provide complementary biomarkers of central and peripheral GABA B Rs engagement and may support translational development of mechanism-based treatments for AUD.

research.title: Positive-affective and negative-cognitive brain-behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis.
research.abstract: Background Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach. Methods Baseline data from 720 CHR participants from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia program (AMP® SCZ) were analyzed using sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify associations between 95 regional brain volumes and 28 behavioral variables indexing symptoms, cognition, and functioning. Generalizability was tested using leave-one-network-out cross-validation (PRoNET and PRESCIENT), and stability was assessed using bootstrapping and leave-one-site-out analyses. Associations with demographic, clinical and site-related variables were examined. Results Two brain-behavior dimensions generalized across networks. A positive-affective axis (r=0.21-0.23), linking higher depression, anxiety/stress, positive symptoms and anhedonia with predominantly frontal-cingulate-insular volume reductions and relatively larger corpus callosum and putamen volumes. This axis was associated with comorbid depression, cannabis use and family history of depression or affective psychosis. A negative-cognitive axis (r=0.17-0.18) linked greater asociality, alogia, emotional withdrawal, blunted affect, and motor retardation, poorer cognition and functioning with reduced cerebellar and parietal volumes, and relatively larger lateral ventricles and corpus callosum. This axis was associated with lower IQ and poorer premorbid adjustment. Conclusions Two partially dissociable brain-behavior dimensions were identified: a positive-affective axis capturing the co-expression of affective and attenuated positive symptoms, and a negative-cognitive axis suggestive of neurodevelopmental vulnerability.

research.title: Effects of childhood maltreatment on emotional intelligence and psychosocial functioning in adult euthymic bipolar disorder patients compared with healthy controls.
research.abstract: Background Childhood maltreatment (CM) has been linked to poor emotional intelligence (EI) and psychosocial functioning (PSF) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD). However, no study has investigated whether EI mediates the relationship between CM and PSF in patients with BD. Here, we aimed to assess the association of CM with EI and PSF in euthymic patients with BD compared with healthy controls (HCs). Methods We assessed 124 euthymic participants with a BD diagnosis and 124 HCs by means of the Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test, the Functioning Assessment Short Test and the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire. Linear regression models were constructed using CM categorized as no-CM, low/moderate-CM and high-CM. We subsequently assessed whether EI mediates the relationship between CM and PSF. Results Compared with HCs, patients with BD reported higher rates of CM and lower rates of PSF and EI. In the BD group, subjects who exhibited low/moderate CM obtained lower levels of PSF and EI than those with no-CM and high-CM levels. The regression models demonstrated that, compared with the no-CM category, the low/moderate CM category was inversely associated with EI strategic area scores in patients with BD. However, EI did not mediate the relationship between CM and PSF. Conclusions Low/moderate-CM was associated with the worst EI scores in BD. However, we did not observe any mediating effect of EI on the relationship between CM and PSF. Our results emphasize the importance of assessing CM in mental health and suggest that targeted therapies should be administered to affected patients.
